title: I made an interactive-fiction engine where Claude writes the story but never rolls the dice
author: Business-Pension-498
selftext:
I made Selkie on my own: an AI writes a novel around your choices, with the bones of a Choice of Games book (chapters, stats, dice with the odds shown, several endings) instead of an open chat.

What I learned:

* **Never let the model roll.** Asked whether you succeed, it nearly always says yes. The engine rolls; the narrator is told the result; the next passage has to show it.
* **Continuity is the hard part.** The worst slips were names the reader had never been told and facts nobody could know yet. A second model now reads each paragraph against the story so far. Its fix goes in before the reader sees it.
* **Most of the work is outside the model.** The clock, the agenda, who has met whom: the engine keeps them and hands the narrator only what this passage needs.

It's live, free to start: [https://playselkie.com/?from=reddit-aigamedev](https://playselkie.com/?from=reddit-aigamedev)

I'd like to hear from anyone building narrative games on LLMs. What broke for you?

comments.author: SwimmerMain2848
comments.body: This is absolutely stunning and I am reading as I type. How can I make sure I can continue on my mobile and not loose a story? Can you make an app out of this?

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body:
Thank you, that's lovely to hear!

Your story's already safe: it saves to your account after every choice. On your phone, go to [app.playselkie.com](http://app.playselkie.com) and sign in the same way you did here (the same email, or the same Google account). Your story will be under Reading, with a Continue button.

App Store and Google Play versions are coming later. Until then you can add it to your home screen. On iPhone, open it in Safari and tap Share → Add to Home Screen. On Android, open it in Chrome and use the ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen. It gets its own icon and opens full screen.

Which story are you reading? And if anything misbehaves on the phone, tell me and I'll fix it.

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body:
Mostly by measuring. Every model call is logged with its tokens and cost, so I know what a turn really costs, and readers pay per turn in ink priced from those numbers. New readers get a small welcome gift; there's no unlimited free tier.

What keeps a turn cheap:

* **Prompt caching.** Everything that doesn't change within a chapter (rules, world, cast) comes first in the prompt and gets cached; the per-turn state comes after it. A cached passage costs about half what an uncached one does.
* **The right model for each job.** The narrator runs on a mid-size model with thinking kept to a minimum, and quick checks like the referee run on a small, fast one. Readers can pick a bigger narrator at a higher ink price.
* **Code does the bookkeeping.** Dice, the clock, stats, who has met whom: the engine handles all of it, and the narrator only gets what this passage needs. Older chapters are summarized instead of sent again.
* **Hard spend limits** on the API side, so a bug can't run up a bill overnight.

The biggest extra is the continuity reader, about 3 cents a passage. I keep it because continuity was the worst problem.

replies.author: Bavariasnaps
replies.body: oh sounds expensive. that can add up for sure.

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body: Ha, yeah, it definitely can! That's why it's the one extra I called out. Two things keep it in check, though. It only reads one paragraph at a time against what the story's already established, and that part stays cached for the whole passage, so most of it is billed at the cheaper cached rate. And honestly, skipping it costs more in the long run: once a reader sees a character know something they couldn't possibly know, they tend to close the tab.

replies.author: Business-Pension-498
replies.body: Thanks😁! If you give it a try, I'd love to hear which story you pick and where it trips up.
